PADUCAH, Kentucky (CNN) -- The aunt of former U.S. soldier Steven Green told jurors tearfully Monday that "We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq" as defense lawyers worked to save her nephew from a death sentence. Former U.S. soldier Steven Green has been convicted of raping and killing a 14-year-old Iraqi girl. Patty Ruth, a Texas elementary school principal, told a civilian jury about Green's childhood as a reader who loved to be hugged by relatives. "I do not know how we got to this spot," Ruth said in emotional testimony. "I do not know how this happened." Green was convicted last week in U.S. District Court in Kentucky of murder, rape, conspiracy and obstruction of justice in connection with a 2006 rape-and-murder south of Baghdad. A jury found him guilty of raping a 14-year-old girl, then killing her and setting her body on fire to destroy evidence. Green also was found guilty of killing the girl's parents and 6-year-old sister. He could become the first former U.S. soldier to face the death penalty for war crimes before a civilian court, where he was tried because he had been discharged from the military before his crimes came to light. Four other former soldiers are in prison for their roles in the crimes and the cover-up that followed. Green faces either death or life in prison without the possibility of parole. His fate will be in the hands of the jury by week's end. The defense has presented relatives and medical professionals who have pieced together a picture of Green's childhood as troubled and stressful. It included the breakup of his parents' marriage, routine beatings to the point of injury by an older brother and being moved about through Texas by his mother. Ruth, the final witness scheduled by the defense, said that when the idea of the military came up for her nephew, she was unsure the Army would accept him. Even after he received a high school diploma through a correspondence course, she said, "I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training." Ruth said when she saw a picture of her nephew before his September 2005 deployment, she knew he wasn't "Stevie" anymore, standing as tall as his father in the photo at Fort Benning, Georgia. When he returned from Iraq 11 months later, he was "remarkably thin," Ruth said, and she noticed circles under his eyes. Green and his father spent a night at the Ruth home, his aunt said, and she remembered him pacing the yard while smoking. He fell asleep wearing his fatigues, she said. When asked by the defense about the rape-murder plot that left an Iraqi family dead near Yusufiya, about 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth responded, "He's my Steve. You can't stop loving someone." There were other family members in the court on Monday. Green's father, John, an oil field worker from Midland, Texas, looked on quietly. He did not testify. Ruth, who is John Green's sister, noted for the jury that Green's mother is not at the trial this week. The mother is moving and had to attend a going-away party, Ruth said. Final arguments are expected Wednesday.

PADUCAH, Kentucky (CNN) — The aunt of former U.S. soldier Steven Green tearfully told jurors Monday, “We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq,” as defense lawyers sought to spare her nephew a death sentence.

Green has been convicted of raping and killing a 14-year-old Iraqi girl. Patty Ruth, a Texas elementary school principal, described to a civilian jury Green’s childhood, portraying him as an avid reader who loved being hugged by relatives.

“I do not know how we got to this spot,” Ruth said in emotional testimony. “I do not know how this happened.”

Green was convicted last week in U.S. District Court in Kentucky of murder, rape, conspiracy, and obstruction of justice in connection with a 2006 rape and murder south of Baghdad. A jury found him guilty of raping a 14-year-old girl, then killing her and setting her body on fire to destroy evidence. Green also was found guilty of killing the girl’s parents and 6-year-old sister.

He could become the first former U.S. soldier to face the death penalty for war crimes before a civilian court. He was tried there because he had been discharged from the military before his crimes came to light. Four other former soldiers are serving prison sentences for their roles in the crimes and the cover-up that followed.

Green faces either death or life in prison without the possibility of parole. His fate is expected to be in the jury’s hands by the end of the week.

The defense has presented testimony from relatives and medical professionals, who have assembled a portrait of Green’s childhood as troubled and stressful. It included the breakup of his parents’ marriage, routine beatings by an older brother that left him injured, and frequent moves around Texas with his mother.

Ruth, the final witness scheduled by the defense, said that when the possibility of military service arose for her nephew, she was uncertain the Army would accept him. Even after he earned a high school diploma through a correspondence course, she said, “I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training.”

Ruth said that when she saw a photograph of her nephew before his September 2005 deployment, she realized he was no longer “Stevie,” standing as tall as his father in the picture taken at Fort Benning, Georgia. When he returned from Iraq 11 months later, he was “remarkably thin,” she said, and she noticed circles under his eyes.

Green and his father spent a night at Ruth’s home, his aunt said, and she recalled him pacing in the yard while smoking. He fell asleep wearing his fatigues, she said.

When asked by the defense about the rape-murder plot that left an Iraqi family dead near Yusufiya, about 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth responded, “He’s my Steve. You can’t stop loving someone.”

Other family members were also present in court Monday. Green’s father, John, an oil field worker from Midland, Texas, looked on quietly but did not testify. Ruth, who is John Green’s sister, told the jury that Green’s mother was not at the trial this week. His mother was moving and had to attend a going-away party, Ruth said.

Final arguments are expected Wednesday.

PADUCAH, Kentucky (CNN) — On Monday, the aunt of former U.S. soldier Steven Green became emotional as she told jurors, “We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq,” while defense attorneys sought to persuade them not to sentence her nephew to death.

Green, a former American soldier, has been found guilty of raping and murdering a 14-year-old Iraqi girl.

Patty Ruth, an elementary school principal from Texas, described Green’s younger years to a civilian jury, portraying him as a child who enjoyed reading and liked receiving hugs from family members. “I do not know how we got to this spot,” Ruth said during tearful testimony. “I do not know how this happened.”

Last week, Green was convicted in U.S. District Court in Kentucky on charges of murder, rape, conspiracy and obstruction of justice related to a 2006 rape and killing south of Baghdad. Jurors determined that he raped the 14-year-old girl, killed her, and then burned her body in an effort to eliminate evidence.

Green was also convicted of murdering the girl’s parents and her 6-year-old sister.

He could be the first former U.S. service member to receive the death penalty for war crimes in a civilian court. He was tried in that setting because he had already been discharged from the military by the time the crimes were uncovered.

Four other former soldiers are serving prison sentences for their involvement in the crimes and the subsequent cover-up.

Green’s sentence will be either death or life in prison without parole. The jury is expected to begin deciding his punishment by the end of the week.

The defense has called relatives and medical experts who have described Green’s upbringing as difficult and unstable. They testified about his parents’ divorce, frequent beatings by an older brother that sometimes caused injuries, and repeated moves around Texas with his mother.

Ruth, the defense’s last scheduled witness, said that when military service was first discussed for Green, she doubted the Army would take him. Even after he earned a high school diploma through a correspondence program, she said, “I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training.”

Ruth said that when she saw a photograph of Green before he deployed in September 2005, she realized he no longer seemed like “Stevie.” In the image, taken at Fort Benning, Georgia, he stood as tall as his father.

When Green came back from Iraq 11 months later, Ruth said, he was “remarkably thin,” and she noticed dark circles beneath his eyes. She testified that Green and his father spent a night at her home, where she recalled seeing him walk back and forth in the yard while smoking. She said he later fell asleep still dressed in his fatigues.

Asked by the defense about the rape-and-murder plan that killed an Iraqi family near Yusufiya, roughly 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth said, “He’s my Steve. You can’t stop loving someone.”

Other relatives were also present in court Monday. Green’s father, John, an oil field worker from Midland, Texas, watched silently but did not take the stand.

Ruth, who is John Green’s sister, pointed out to jurors that Green’s mother was not attending the trial that week. Ruth said his mother was moving and had to go to a farewell party.

Closing arguments are expected on Wednesday.

During the penalty phase, Green’s defense team sought to persuade jurors that his life should be spared, presenting testimony about his background, family history and mental health. His aunt’s testimony was among the most personal, as she spoke through tears about Green’s upbringing and the instability he faced before entering the Army.

Defense attorneys have argued that while the crimes were horrific, Green’s personal history and psychological condition are reasons to impose life in prison without parole rather than capital punishment. They have also pointed to the stresses of war and Green’s young age at the time of the killings as mitigating factors.

Prosecutors, however, have urged the jury to impose the death penalty, emphasizing the brutality of the attack and the vulnerability of the victims. They have described the killings as premeditated and calculated, arguing that Green deserves the harshest punishment available under federal law.

The case has drawn international attention because it is one of the rare instances in which a former U.S. service member was tried in a civilian federal court for crimes committed while deployed overseas. Several other soldiers were prosecuted in military courts for their roles in the attack.

Jurors must now decide whether Green should be sentenced to death or spend the rest of his life in prison without the possibility of release.

**Former U.S. Soldier Steven Green Convicted in 2006 Yusufiya Rape-Murder Case; Jury to Consider Possible Death Sentence**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*Louisville, Kentucky — [Date]*

A federal jury has convicted former U.S. Army soldier **Steven Dale Green** for his role in one of the most notorious crimes committed by American troops during the Iraq War: the 2006 rape of a 14-year-old Iraqi girl and the murders of her and three members of her family near Yusufiya, south of Baghdad.

Green, a former private with the 101st Airborne Division, was found guilty in U.S. District Court in Kentucky of charges including murder, rape and obstruction of justice in connection with the attack on **Abeer Qassim al-Janabi**, her parents and her younger sister. The case, often referred to as the **Yusufiya rape-murder case** or the **Mahmudiyah killings**, shocked both Iraq and the United States and became a symbol of the strain, brutality and moral collapse that could occur amid repeated combat deployments and weak discipline.

Prosecutors alleged that Green and several fellow soldiers planned the attack after drinking alcohol at a checkpoint. According to testimony, Green and others went to the family’s home, where Green shot Abeer’s parents and younger sister before Abeer was raped and killed. The house was then set on fire in an effort to conceal the crime.

Because Green had been discharged from the Army before the full allegations emerged, he was tried in civilian federal court rather than by court-martial. Other soldiers involved in the crime were prosecuted in the military justice system and received lengthy prison sentences after plea agreements or convictions.

### Aunt Describes a Troubled Young Man

Outside the legal proceedings, Green’s family history has drawn attention as jurors prepare to weigh whether he should receive the death penalty. His aunt, **Patty Ruth**, has spoken publicly about Green’s difficult upbringing, describing him as a troubled young man whose life had been marked by instability, emotional problems and poor choices long before he entered the Army.

Ruth has portrayed the family as devastated by the crimes while also urging people to understand that Green did not emerge from a stable background. Her comments have not excused the killings, but they have become part of the broader portrait defense attorneys are expected to present as they argue for mercy during the sentencing phase.

Green’s lawyers have pointed to his troubled childhood, substance abuse, psychological struggles and alleged failures by the Army to screen and supervise him properly. They have argued that he was sent into a combat environment despite clear signs that he was emotionally unfit and had a history of alcohol and drug problems.

### A Troubled Background Before the Army

Green’s past has figured heavily in the case. Reports and court filings have described him as someone who struggled with authority, drinking and drug use before enlisting. He reportedly came from a fractured family environment and had brushes with the law before joining the military.

Like many recruits during the height of the Iraq War, Green entered the Army at a time when the military was under pressure to meet recruitment needs. His defense team has suggested that warning signs were overlooked and that he should never have been placed in a volatile combat role.

Prosecutors, however, have argued that Green’s background does not diminish his responsibility for a deliberate and exceptionally brutal crime. They have emphasized the calculated nature of the attack: the decision to leave the checkpoint, target a civilian family, kill witnesses and attempt to cover up the evidence.

### Death Penalty Possible

The conviction moves the case into a penalty phase, where jurors must decide whether Green should be sentenced to death or spend the rest of his life in prison. Federal prosecutors have sought the death penalty, arguing that the murders were premeditated and accompanied by aggravated factors, including rape, the killing of a child and the attempt to destroy evidence by burning the victims’ home.

For a death sentence to be imposed in federal court, the jury must make specific findings and reach a unanimous decision. If jurors cannot agree on death, Green would face a life sentence without the possibility of release.

The sentencing decision is expected to focus on two competing narratives: the prosecution’s depiction of Green as the central figure in a planned atrocity against civilians, and the defense’s portrayal of him as a deeply damaged young soldier placed in a war zone despite obvious warning signs.

### A Case That Reverberated Beyond the Courtroom

The Yusufiya case caused outrage in Iraq, where it fed public anger toward U.S. forces and intensified scrutiny of American military conduct. It also led to renewed questions in the United States about combat stress, military discipline, recruitment standards and accountability for crimes committed overseas.

For Abeer’s surviving relatives and many Iraqis, the conviction represents a measure of justice but not closure. The killings destroyed an entire family and left a lasting stain on the U.S. military’s legacy in Iraq.

As the court turns to the question of punishment, Green’s fate will rest with the jury: whether he should be executed for the crimes or imprisoned for life.

## Former Soldier Convicted in Iraq Family Killings; Aunt Says, “We Did Not Send a Rapist and Murderer to Iraq”

**PADUCAH, Kentucky —** A former U.S. soldier was convicted in federal court for his role in one of the most notorious crimes committed by American troops during the Iraq War: the rape and murder of a teenage Iraqi girl and the killing of her family south of Baghdad.

A jury found **Steven Dale Green**, a former Army private, guilty in connection with the 2006 attack in **Mahmoudiya**, a rural area south of the Iraqi capital. Prosecutors said Green and other soldiers targeted a family living near a military checkpoint, killing the girl’s parents and younger sister before raping and murdering the teenager, identified in court records and reports as **Abeer Qassim al-Janabi**.

The case shocked military officials, devastated Iraqis already living amid war, and became a symbol of the worst abuses carried out by individual U.S. service members during the conflict.

Outside the courtroom, Green’s family struggled to reconcile the man they knew with the crimes described in court. His aunt, speaking through grief and disbelief, offered a statement that underscored the family’s anguish:

**“We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq.”**

The remark captured a central tension running through the trial: whether Green was a willing participant in a brutal crime or a damaged young man transformed by war, military culture, and psychological decline. Prosecutors argued that the evidence showed planning, intent, and cruelty. Defense attorneys sought to portray Green as mentally unstable and deeply affected by his deployment.

### A Crime That Stunned Iraq and the U.S. Military

The killings occurred in March 2006 in a village near Mahmoudiya, where U.S. soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division were stationed amid heavy insurgent activity. According to testimony and court filings, Green and several fellow soldiers left their post, changed into dark clothing, and went to the home of the al-Janabi family.

Prosecutors said Green shot and killed the girl’s parents and younger sister, while Abeer was raped and then killed. The home was set on fire in an apparent attempt to destroy evidence.

The crime initially was believed to be the work of insurgents. But investigators later uncovered the involvement of U.S. soldiers after another service member came forward. Several soldiers pleaded guilty in military proceedings and testified against Green.

Green had been discharged from the Army before the allegations fully emerged, which meant he was prosecuted in civilian federal court rather than by court-martial. The case was tried in Kentucky because Green was from the state and had been living there after his discharge.

### Prosecutors: “Premeditated” and “Brutal”

Federal prosecutors described the attack as calculated and deliberate, saying Green and the other soldiers singled out the family after seeing the teenage girl near their checkpoint.

They argued that the killings were not a spontaneous battlefield incident, nor a tragic mistake amid combat, but a planned attack against unarmed civilians.

The evidence presented at trial included testimony from former soldiers who admitted participating in the crime. Their accounts placed Green at the center of the violence, particularly in the shooting deaths of the family members.

### Defense: War Damaged Him

Green’s attorneys did not deny the horror of the killings, but they emphasized his mental state, his troubled background, and the psychological toll of deployment. They argued that Green had been failed by the Army and was not properly screened or treated before or during his time in Iraq.

The defense portrayed him as a young man exposed to relentless danger, stress, and trauma — someone who should not have been in a war zone.

That argument echoed the sentiment expressed by his aunt, whose statement — **“We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq”** — suggested that the family believed Green had changed dramatically after enlistment and deployment.

But prosecutors rejected the idea that combat stress could explain or excuse the crime. They said many soldiers faced danger and trauma in Iraq without committing atrocities.

### A Painful Verdict

The conviction brought a measure of legal accountability, but little comfort to those who followed the case in Iraq and the United States. For Iraqis, the murders reinforced anger over civilian casualties, night raids, checkpoints, and the conduct of foreign troops occupying their communities.

For the U.S. military, the case became a grim reminder of the importance of discipline, oversight, and accountability in war zones.

Green was later sentenced to life in prison after jurors did not impose the death penalty. He died in federal custody in 2014.

The other soldiers involved received lengthy prison sentences through the military justice system.

### A Lasting Stain

Years after the killings, the Mahmoudiya case remains one of the darkest chapters of the Iraq War. It stands apart not because civilians died — a frequent tragedy in the conflict — but because prosecutors said the family was deliberately targeted, the teenage girl was sexually assaulted, and the murders were carried out by those assigned to protect the area.

The words of Green’s aunt continue to resonate because they reflect the disbelief felt by many families of service members accused of wartime crimes: the fear that the person who returned was not the person who left.

**“We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq,”** she said.

For the family of Abeer Qassim al-Janabi, however, the question was never only what war did to an American soldier. It was what that soldier and his fellow troops did to an Iraqi family — and why no explanation could undo it.
